newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Pre-handover election fever sweeps idyllic HK isle.
newsitem.headline: Pre-handover election fever sweeps idyllic HK isle.

text.p: Election fever gripped scenic Cheung Chau island on Sunday in Hong Kong's last major grassroots ballot before Chinese rule on July 1.
The sleepy little isle, nearly an hour's ferry-ride southwest from metropolitan Hong Kong, staged local elections, demonstrating confidence in a future shadowed by uncertainty.
Folks say it was Cheung Chau's biggest day of mass action since local windsurfer-heroine Lee Lai-shan sparked rejoicing by winning Hong Kong's sole gold medal at the 1996 Olympics.

"Exercise your precious right to vote," said posters in red, gold and purple as islanders streamed to the Way Yan Buddhist Memorial College where officials supervised two scarlet, heavily-padlocked voting boxes.

"We don't mind about the future -- it's reunification with the motherland, China," chorused voters emerging from the central polling booth near the waterside township where candidates' backers handed out soft drinks and slogans.

Cheung Chau, an idyllic retreat of beaches and hills without any motorcars or highways, has only one other big day, an annual "bun festival" in early May when people climb high bamboo poles for lucky bread buns.
Cycle-drawn rickshaws, the local taxis, are about as fast as life's pace gets here, in contrast to bustling urban Hong Kong.
No one interviewed at the election -- disregarded by the rest of Hong Kong as too local to be of interest -- echoed any of the standard Western fears about the next few decades.
China has made a "hands-off" pledge to retain for 50 years capitalism when Hong Kong, a territory of 6.4 million people, mostly Chinese, gets some autonomy at the end of British colonial rule.
An omen for its appointment with destiny figured in classroom noticeboards for the island's secondary school pupils -- miniatures of the five-starred communist flag of the People's Republic of China.
A mass showing of the red flag, still seen in just a handful of places in Hong Kong, will mark the end of British rule in 37 days.

Officials say the islanders, fishing-crew descendants of pirates who roamed the South China Sea, are already learning China's national song, whose key words "qi lai" (rise up) starkly contrast with the British anthem "God Save the Queen."
Governor Chris Patten angered Beijing by introducing mild democratic reforms, including a wider election franchise, to Hong Kong in 1995.
Effectively for Cheung Chau, this has meant votes for women for the first time.
Previously the dumbbell-shaped island of 30,000 people voted for its Rural Committee, as the bedrock local administration is known, on a single vote per household basis.
"As most household chiefs were traditionally male, this virtually excluded women from voting," said District Officer K.B Wong.

Wong, 40, a career civil servant who is effectively the island's chief executive, said: "We have universal franchise now. We are still learning our way but we hope for an accountable and secure future."
He ran the electoral process from a school classroom whose door carried a college sign: "Discipline and guidance unit."

"Everyone, 18 and over with seven years residence can vote now," said Wong, as people streamed through the college gymnasium to vote by a door marked "Tuck Shop" -- a British school term for the pupils' candy shop.
Turnout of the 7,000-strong electorate was reported good in brilliant sunshine that drew boatloads of day-trippers from the main Hong Kong island.

"The democratic system will go on, I believe," said businessman Eric Ho, after voting. "Yes it will continue," said housewife Cheung Sheng-fai. "This is a better system than what we had, though it is more complicated," said hospital volunteer Kwok Tai-fook.
To fill five vacancies, voters selected on personal quality rather than party platforms from eight candidates, two of them women.
A part-time magistrate, Wong, 40, represents Hong Kong's new democracy-committed generation whose parents had no direct voice in affairs under Britain's benign but unrepresentative rule.
Hong Kongers believe the process is irreversible, he says.
The Rural Committee has 35 members, including two women, and polls are held periodically as incumbents occasionally resign, lacking time to serve a full term.

To complete an electoral process in Hong Kong's New Territories, bordering the Chinese mainland, similar though smaller polls are likely on other islands in the next two years -- a test of China's avowed good faith.
